parts.text: Which one of the following best describes **scarcity**?
choices: The next best alternative forgone/given up when a choice is made
The situation where resources are limited/finite while wants are unlimited, so choices must be made
Natural resources used in production, such as minerals, soil, forests and water
The resources/inputs used to produce goods and services namely land, labour, capital and enterprise

rows.answer:
Correct option: **B** (The situation where resources are limited/finite while wants are unlimited, so choices must be made)
A: incorrect, that is the meaning of opportunity cost
C: incorrect, that is the meaning of land
D: incorrect, that is the meaning of factors of production

parts.text: Which one of the following best describes **production possibility curve (PPC)**?
choices: A curve showing the maximum combinations of two goods/services that can be produced when all resources are fully and efficiently used
The amount of one good that must be given up to produce more of the other good when moving along the curve
A combination of goods outside the curve which cannot be produced with the current resources and technology
Producing at a point on the PPC so it is not possible to produce more of one good without producing less of the other

rows.notes: Award 1 mark for a precise definition. Do not award the mark for an example alone.

parts.text: What is meant by the term **productive efficiency (on a PPC)**?

rows.answer: Producing at a point on the PPC (1) so it is not possible to produce more of one good without producing less of the other (1).
rows.notes: Award 1 mark for each element of the definition. Do not award marks for examples.

parts.text: Define the term **an unattainable point on a PPC**.

rows.answer: A combination of goods outside the curve which cannot be produced with the current resources and technology.
rows.notes: Award 1 mark for a precise definition. Do not award the mark for an example alone.

parts.text: What is meant by the term **an unattainable point on a PPC**?

rows.answer: A combination of goods outside the curve (1) which cannot be produced with the current resources and technology (1).
rows.notes: Award 1 mark for each element of the definition. Do not award marks for examples.

parts.text: Define the term **economic growth (shown on a PPC)**.

rows.answer: An outward shift of the PPC showing an increase in the productive capacity of the economy.
rows.notes: Award 1 mark for a precise definition. Do not award the mark for an example alone.

parts.text: What is meant by the term **economic growth (shown on a PPC)**?

rows.answer: An outward shift of the PPC (1) showing an increase in the productive capacity of the economy (1).
rows.notes: Award 1 mark for each element of the definition. Do not award marks for examples.

parts.text: Define the term **unemployment of resources (on a PPC)**.

rows.answer: A point inside the PPC where some resources are idle or used inefficiently.
rows.notes: Award 1 mark for a precise definition. Do not award the mark for an example alone.

parts.text: What is meant by the term **unemployment of resources (on a PPC)**?

rows.answer: A point inside the PPC (1) where some resources are idle or used inefficiently (1).
rows.notes: Award 1 mark for each element of the definition. Do not award marks for examples.

parts.text: Define the term **opportunity cost (on a PPC)**.

rows.answer: The amount of one good that must be given up to produce more of the other good when moving along the curve.
rows.notes: Award 1 mark for a precise definition. Do not award the mark for an example alone.

parts.text: What is meant by the term **opportunity cost (on a PPC)**?

rows.answer: The amount of one good that must be given up (1) to produce more of the other good when moving along the curve (1).
rows.notes: Award 1 mark for each element of the definition. Do not award marks for examples.

Describe one way advertising can affect the demand for a product.

rows.answer:
Award 1 mark for a relevant point and 1 mark for a linked development, for example:
- advertising makes more consumers aware of the product (1) shifting the demand curve to the right (1)
- advertising can build brand loyalty (1) so consumers keep buying even if rivals cut prices (1)
rows.notes: Only one point should be credited. A second, undeveloped point does not gain the development mark.

parts.text: Which one of the following best describes **supply**?
choices: A rise in quantity supplied caused by a rise in the price of the product (movement up the supply curve)
A fall in quantity supplied caused by a fall in the price of the product (movement down the supply curve)
The amount of a product that firms are prepared to offer for sale at each price over a period of time
A tax on spending/goods and services which raises firms' costs and reduces supply

rows.answer:
Correct option: **C** (The amount of a product that firms are prepared to offer for sale at each price over a period of time)
A: incorrect, that is the meaning of an extension in supply
B: incorrect, that is the meaning of a contraction in supply
D: incorrect, that is the meaning of an indirect tax

A: incorrect, that is the meaning of a contraction in supply

parts.text: Define the term **supply**.

rows.answer: The amount of a product that firms are prepared to offer for sale at each price over a period of time.
rows.notes: Award 1 mark for a precise definition. Do not award the mark for an example alone.

parts.text: What is meant by the term **supply**?

parts.text: Which one of the following best describes **equilibrium price**?
choices: Any place or arrangement where buyers and sellers come together to exchange goods or services
The price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied

When quantity supplied is greater than quantity demanded at a price above the equilibrium

parts.text: Which one of the following best describes **price elasticity of demand (PED)**?
choices: The money a firm receives from selling its output calculated as price multiplied by quantity sold
When a change in price leads to a proportionately larger change in quantity demanded (PED greater than 1, ignoring the sign)
A measure of how strongly the amount bought reacts when the price of the product changes
When a change in price leads to a proportionately equal change in quantity demanded (PED = 1, ignoring the sign)

rows.answer:
Correct option: **C** (A measure of how strongly the amount bought reacts when the price of the product changes)
A: incorrect, that is the meaning of total revenue
B: incorrect, that is the meaning of price elastic demand
D: incorrect, that is the meaning of unitary elastic demand

parts.text: Which one of the following best describes **price elastic demand**?
choices: When a change in price leads to a proportionately smaller change in quantity demanded (PED less than 1, ignoring the sign)
When a change in price leads to a proportionately larger change in quantity demanded (PED greater than 1, ignoring the sign)
When quantity demanded does not change at all whatever happens to price (PED = 0)
The money a firm receives from selling its output calculated as price multiplied by quantity sold

rows.answer:
Correct option: **B** (When a change in price leads to a proportionately larger change in quantity demanded (PED greater than 1, ignoring the sign))
A: incorrect, that is the meaning of price inelastic demand
C: incorrect, that is the meaning of perfectly inelastic demand
D: incorrect, that is the meaning of total revenue

Correct option: **D** (When a change in price leads to a proportionately smaller change in quantity demanded (PED less than 1, ignoring the sign))

C: incorrect, that is the meaning of income elasticity of demand (YED)

parts.text: Describe one factor that affects the price elasticity of demand for a product.

rows.answer:
Award 1 mark for a relevant point and 1 mark for a linked development, for example:
- the number of substitutes (1): the more close substitutes there are, the more elastic demand is because consumers can switch easily (1)
- whether it is a necessity (1): necessities tend to have inelastic demand because consumers need them whatever the price (1)
- the proportion of income spent (1): goods that take a large share of income tend to have more elastic demand (1)
rows.notes: Only one point should be credited. A second, undeveloped point does not gain the development mark.

parts.text: Which one of the following best describes **price elasticity of supply (PES)**?
choices: The responsiveness of quantity supplied to a change in price
When a firm is producing less than the maximum it could with its existing resources
When a change in price causes a proportionately smaller change in quantity supplied (PES less than 1)
When quantity supplied cannot change whatever the price (PES = 0)

rows.answer:
Correct option: **A** (The responsiveness of quantity supplied to a change in price)
B: incorrect, that is the meaning of spare capacity
C: incorrect, that is the meaning of price inelastic supply
D: incorrect, that is the meaning of perfectly inelastic supply

parts.text: Which one of the following best describes **price elastic supply**?
choices: When a change in price causes a proportionately larger change in quantity supplied (PES greater than 1)
When a firm is producing less than the maximum it could with its existing resources
When quantity supplied cannot change whatever the price (PES = 0)
When a change in price causes a proportionately smaller change in quantity supplied (PES less than 1)

rows.answer:
Correct option: **A** (When a change in price causes a proportionately larger change in quantity supplied (PES greater than 1))
B: incorrect, that is the meaning of spare capacity
C: incorrect, that is the meaning of perfectly inelastic supply
D: incorrect, that is the meaning of price inelastic supply

parts.text: Which one of the following best describes **price inelastic supply**?
choices: The responsiveness of quantity supplied to a change in price
When a change in price causes a proportionately larger change in quantity supplied (PES greater than 1)
When a change in price causes a proportionately smaller change in quantity supplied (PES less than 1)
Goods that have been produced and stored so they can be sold later

rows.answer:
Correct option: **C** (When a change in price causes a proportionately smaller change in quantity supplied (PES less than 1))
A: incorrect, that is the meaning of price elasticity of supply (PES)
B: incorrect, that is the meaning of price elastic supply
D: incorrect, that is the meaning of stock (inventory)

parts.text: Which one of the following best describes **spare capacity**?
choices: When a firm is producing less than the maximum it could with its existing resources
When quantity supplied cannot change whatever the price (PES = 0)
Goods that have been produced and stored so they can be sold later
When a change in price causes a proportionately smaller change in quantity supplied (PES less than 1)

rows.answer:
Correct option: **A** (When a firm is producing less than the maximum it could with its existing resources)
B: incorrect, that is the meaning of perfectly inelastic supply
C: incorrect, that is the meaning of stock (inventory)
D: incorrect, that is the meaning of price inelastic supply

parts.text: Which one of the following best describes **stock (inventory)**?
choices: When quantity supplied cannot change whatever the price (PES = 0)

parts.text:
Riverstone Partners produces bottled water in Glasgow. Its factory currently uses only 56% of its capacity.

Explain why the supply of Riverstone Partners's bottled water is likely to be price elastic.

rows.answer:
Award 1 mark for identifying a relevant point, 1 mark for developing it and 1 mark for applying it to the context.

Example:
- Riverstone Partners has spare capacity (1) because 56% of capacity is used (1), so if the price of bottled water rises it can increase output quickly using idle machines and workers (1)
rows.notes: Accept any other valid explanation. Answers with no reference to the context cannot gain the third mark.

parts.text: Which one of the following best describes **mixed economy**?
choices: The part of the economy owned and controlled by individuals and private firms, mainly aiming for profit
An economy where resources are allocated by the price mechanism with little or no government intervention
A good that is under-consumed in a free market because people underestimate its benefits, such as education
An economy in which resources are allocated by both the private sector and the public/state sector

rows.answer:
Correct option: **D** (An economy in which resources are allocated by both the private sector and the public/state sector)
A: incorrect, that is the meaning of private sector
B: incorrect, that is the meaning of free market economy
C: incorrect, that is the meaning of merit good

parts.text: Which one of the following best describes **private sector**?
choices: The part of the economy owned and controlled by the government/state
The part of the economy owned and controlled by individuals and private firms, mainly aiming for profit
When people benefit from a good without paying for it, so firms cannot charge for it
An economy where resources are allocated by the price mechanism with little or no government intervention

rows.answer:
Correct option: **B** (The part of the economy owned and controlled by individuals and private firms, mainly aiming for profit)
A: incorrect, that is the meaning of public sector
C: incorrect, that is the meaning of free-rider problem
D: incorrect, that is the meaning of free market economy

parts.text: Which one of the following best describes **public sector**?
choices: A good that is under-consumed in a free market because people underestimate its benefits, such as education
An economy where resources are allocated by the price mechanism with little or no government intervention
The part of the economy owned and controlled by the government/state
An economy in which resources are allocated by both the private sector and the public/state sector

rows.answer:
Correct option: **C** (The part of the economy owned and controlled by the government/state)
A: incorrect, that is the meaning of merit good
B: incorrect, that is the meaning of free market economy
D: incorrect, that is the meaning of mixed economy

parts.text: Which one of the following best describes **public good**?
choices: The part of the economy owned and controlled by individuals and private firms, mainly aiming for profit
An economy where resources are allocated by the price mechanism with little or no government intervention
The part of the economy owned and controlled by the government/state
A good that is non-excludable and non-rival so it would not be provided by the free market

rows.answer:
Correct option: **D** (A good that is non-excludable and non-rival so it would not be provided by the free market)
A: incorrect, that is the meaning of private sector
B: incorrect, that is the meaning of free market economy
C: incorrect, that is the meaning of public sector

parts.text: Which one of the following best describes **free market economy**?
choices: A good that is non-excludable and non-rival so it would not be provided by the free market
When people benefit from a good without paying for it, so firms cannot charge for it
An economy where resources are allocated by the price mechanism with little or no government intervention
A good that is under-consumed in a free market because people underestimate its benefits, such as education

A: incorrect, that is the meaning of public good

Accurate knowledge applied consistently, making effective use of the context and data. Chains of reasoning are well developed and balanced. Evaluation is sustained and reaches a clear, supported judgement, for example by weighing short-run against long-run effects or considering what the outcome depends on.

indicative: AO2/AO3: Street lighting is a public good: non-excludable and non-rival
AO2/AO3: Firms cannot charge users because of the free-rider problem, so they cannot make a profit
AO2/AO3: The market fails to provide it, so there is under-provision
AO2/AO3: Better lighting may reduce crime, giving benefits to the whole community
AO4: Government spending on lighting has an opportunity cost

intro: Towns in Istrova have poor street lighting and local residents say crime has increased. Private firms have refused to install lighting because they say they cannot make a profit from it.

parts.text: An indirect tax on a product will shift
choices: the demand curve to the right
the supply curve to the right
the supply curve to the left
the demand curve to the left

rows.answer:
Correct option: **C** (the supply curve to the left)
A: incorrect
B: incorrect
D: incorrect

parts.text: A subsidy to producers is likely to result in
choices: no change in price
a lower price and a higher quantity
a higher price and higher quantity
a higher price and lower quantity

rows.answer:
Correct option: **B** (a lower price and a higher quantity)
A: incorrect
C: incorrect
D: incorrect

parts.text: Define the term **indirect tax**.

rows.answer: A tax on spending on goods and services collected from firms, which raises costs and reduces supply.
rows.notes: Award 1 mark for a precise definition. Do not award the mark for an example alone.

parts.text: What is meant by the term **indirect tax**?

rows.answer: A tax on spending on goods and services (1) collected from firms, which raises costs and reduces supply (1).
rows.notes: Award 1 mark for each element of the definition. Do not award marks for examples.

parts.text: Define the term **subsidy**.

rows.answer: A payment by the government to producers to reduce their costs and increase supply.
rows.notes: Award 1 mark for a precise definition. Do not award the mark for an example alone.

parts.text: What is meant by the term **subsidy**?

rows.answer: A payment by the government to producers (1) to reduce their costs and increase supply (1).

parts.text: Define the term **regulation**.

parts.text: Which one of the following best describes **externality**?
choices: The total cost to society of an activity equal to private cost plus external cost
A benefit to third parties from the production or consumption of a good, such as from vaccination
A cost or benefit to a third party not involved in the production or consumption of a good
The cost of an activity paid by third parties rather than the producer or consumer

rows.answer:
Correct option: **C** (A cost or benefit to a third party not involved in the production or consumption of a good)
A: incorrect, that is the meaning of social cost
B: incorrect, that is the meaning of positive externality
D: incorrect, that is the meaning of external cost

parts.text: Which one of the following best describes **negative externality**?
choices: The cost of an activity paid by the individual or firm carrying it out
The total cost to society of an activity equal to private cost plus external cost
A cost to third parties from the production or consumption of a good, such as pollution
The total benefit to society of an activity equal to private benefit plus external benefit

rows.answer:
Correct option: **C** (A cost to third parties from the production or consumption of a good, such as pollution)
A: incorrect, that is the meaning of private cost
B: incorrect, that is the meaning of social cost
D: incorrect, that is the meaning of social benefit

parts.text: Define the term **externality**.

rows.answer: A cost or benefit to a third party not involved in the production or consumption of a good.
rows.notes: Award 1 mark for a precise definition. Do not award the mark for an example alone.

parts.text: What is meant by the term **externality**?

rows.answer: A cost or benefit to a third party (1) not involved in the production or consumption of a good (1).
rows.notes: Award 1 mark for each element of the definition. Do not award marks for examples.

parts.text: Define the term **negative externality**.

rows.answer: A cost to third parties from the production or consumption of a good, such as pollution.
rows.notes: Award 1 mark for a precise definition. Do not award the mark for an example alone.

parts.text: What is meant by the term **negative externality**?

rows.answer: A cost to third parties (1) from the production or consumption of a good, such as pollution (1).
rows.notes: Award 1 mark for each element of the definition. Do not award marks for examples.

parts.text: Define the term **positive externality**.

rows.answer: A benefit to third parties from the production or consumption of a good, such as from vaccination.
rows.notes: Award 1 mark for a precise definition. Do not award the mark for an example alone.

parts.text: What is meant by the term **positive externality**?

rows.answer: A benefit to third parties (1) from the production or consumption of a good, such as from vaccination (1).
rows.notes: Award 1 mark for each element of the definition. Do not award marks for examples.

parts.text: Define the term **social cost**.

rows.answer: The total cost to society of an activity equal to private cost plus external cost.
rows.notes: Award 1 mark for a precise definition. Do not award the mark for an example alone.

parts.text: What is meant by the term **social cost**?

rows.answer: The total cost to society of an activity (1) equal to private cost plus external cost (1).
rows.notes: Award 1 mark for each element of the definition. Do not award marks for examples.

parts.text: Define the term **social benefit**.

rows.notes: Award 1 mark for a precise definition. Do not award the mark for an example alone.

parts.text: What is meant by the term **social benefit**?

rows.answer: The total benefit to society of an activity (1) equal to private benefit plus external benefit (1).
rows.notes: Award 1 mark for each element of the definition. Do not award marks for examples.

parts.text: Define the term **private cost**.

rows.answer: The cost of an activity paid by the individual or firm carrying it out.
rows.notes: Award 1 mark for a precise definition. Do not award the mark for an example alone.

parts.text: What is meant by the term **private cost**?

rows.answer: The cost of an activity (1) paid by the individual or firm carrying it out (1).
rows.notes: Award 1 mark for each element of the definition. Do not award marks for examples.

parts.text: Define the term **external cost**.

rows.answer: The cost of an activity paid by third parties rather than the producer or consumer.
rows.notes: Award 1 mark for a precise definition. Do not award the mark for an example alone.

parts.text: What is meant by the term **external cost**?

rows.answer: The cost of an activity (1) paid by third parties rather than the producer or consumer (1).
rows.notes: Award 1 mark for each element of the definition. Do not award marks for examples.

parts.text: Define the term **fine**.

rows.answer: A financial penalty imposed on a firm or individual for breaking a rule or law.

parts.text: What is meant by the term **fine**?

rows.answer: A financial penalty (1) imposed on a firm or individual for breaking a rule or law (1).
rows.notes: Award 1 mark for each element of the definition. Do not award marks for examples.

parts.text: Describe one reason why a government might subsidise vaccinations.

rows.notes: Only one point should be credited. A second, undeveloped point does not gain the development mark.

parts.text:
Silverleaf Partners operates a cement works on the edge of Lyon. Residents have complained about dust and lorry traffic.

Explain one negative externality caused by Silverleaf Partners.

rows.answer:
Award 1 mark for identifying a relevant point, 1 mark for developing it and 1 mark for applying it to the context.

Example:
- Dust pollution (1) is a cost to third parties because residents of Lyon suffer breathing problems and dirtier homes (1), which Silverleaf Partners does not pay for, so social cost is higher than private cost (1)
rows.notes: Accept any other valid explanation. Answers with no reference to the context cannot gain the third mark.
